cim: Artificial Intelligence Thoughts Of The Week
cim_eredeti: Artificial Intelligence Thoughts Of The Week
szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial Intelligence is so hot, it has earned its own Thoughts of the Week column.

“Bank of America’s latest fund manager survey shows technology exposure falling at its fastest monthly pace in two decades, with 38% of respondents concerned that companies are overinvesting in artificial intelligence. I see this as a reassessment of valuations and capital efficiency rather than a wholesale rejection of technology. “For much of the past two years, investors have been willing to finance growth based on expectations of future (Artificial Intelligence) demand. That becomes harder to justify when borrowing costs remain elevated and the returns on infrastructure investment are still developing. Institutional investors are becoming more selective about where they deploy capital, and I expect that discipline to extend into digital assets.”

– Ryan Kirkley, co-founder and CEO, Global Settlement Network

“The concerns surrounding Nvidia’s leadership and the financing of smaller AI cloud providers raise a broader question about how much of the technology sector’s growth depends on continued access to inexpensive capital. “Artificial Intelligence demand can remain strong while the economics of financing that demand become increasingly difficult. Smaller infrastructure providers carrying significant debt are particularly exposed if lenders demand higher returns or investors become less willing to finance expansion. That creates risks beyond individual companies, particularly where financing arrangements and infrastructure investments are interconnected.

“Putting agent control in place is very important. Across the industry, people sometimes conflate quite a few layers, all bundled into ‘agent trust.’ But in fact, handling agent risk and making sure an agent is trustworthy comes with a lot of components:

1. Security/cybersecurity layer: Typically tied to ensuring the APIs and the agent are not easily hacked. 2. Identity and authorization: Ensuring that the agent is tied to a human being and behaves under human instruction. 3. Runtime risk assessment: When an agent actually performs financial activities (such as making a transaction on X402), making sure the human’s intent and the agent’s mandate are perfectly aligned, and that the counterparty, payment rails, and all other critical components are properly validated. 4. Liability and dispute: Handling how we address things if something goes wrong. I think the biggest challenge right now is that the industry is still in the midst of worrying about agent financial risk without diving deep to look back at our human-centric infrastructure and how to make it more agent-compatible, particularly on the risk assessment and trust layer.”

“One of the next big fights in enterprise Artificial Intelligence will not be about whether the technology works. It will be about who tells the business that using the cheapest LLM model may be a bad idea.

“As AI usage scales, token costs are about to matter a lot. Business teams will inevitably ask why they are paying premium prices for proprietary models when cheaper open-weight alternatives can do the job. Then somebody will suggest a Chinese model that performs remarkably well for a fraction of the cost.

“Congratulations, security teams, you inherit the mantle of yes, but there are serious cybersecurity concerns with that decision. The problem is that cheaper tokens do not magically erase questions about model provenance, training data, intellectual property, privacy, or supply chain risk.

“I call this the ‘fruit of the poisonous LLM.’ If you do not understand what sits inside the model, everything built on top of it may inherit risks you never priced into that bargain. Moreover, the US government may decide to ban Chinese models based on national security or other concerns.

“Tokenomics will increasingly drive AI architecture. Security teams need to understand that economic pressure now, because waiting until the CFO champions the cheaper model makes for a tough AI governance strategy.”

–Dr. Darren Williams, founder and CEO, BlackFog

“In 2027, I expect more security teams to set limits on what AI agents can do based on the consequences for the business. A security agent might be allowed to isolate one employee laptop when it sees evidence of compromise. Before it isolates enough laptops to interrupt an entire department’s work, someone with the authority to make that call should approve it.

“I’d start by looking at the actions agents can already take and asking which decisions you’re comfortable delegating. Then decide when a person needs to step in, and enforce that boundary when the agent attempts the action. A series of individually permitted actions can add up to an outage.”

“In 2027, I expect more security teams to test whether they can reconstruct an AI agent’s actions before approving it to make consequential changes. Say an agent changes a firewall rule and exposes an internal service. Can the incident response team trace that change back to a person’s request, an instruction embedded in a document the agent read, or an error in the workflow?

“A tabletop exercise is a good way to find out. Pick one workflow and ask the team to reconstruct a run using the evidence they have today. Can they tell what the agent read, which tool it called, whose permissions it used, and what actually changed? Each gap tells you something specific to fix before you give the agent more authority.”

– Caroline Wong, chief strategy officer, Axari, and faculty, IANS

“Cybersecurity costs will grow, but many organizations may experience diminishing returns on their security investments. We cannot effectively secure our systems and data without understanding, at a fundamental technical level, how AI models and agents function and how they can be manipulated or exploited.

“Security leaders may let vendors dictate the solutions, but vendors may offer solutions to problems organizations don’t even have. Attack surfaces may continue to grow due to unaddressed vulnerabilities in AI models and agents. The question organizations need to ask is: Do we have the technical expertise to adequately identify, assess, and manage these risks?”

“The private sector will need to lead by example by establishing consensus-based, industry-led AI governance standards. If the industry fails to establish effective standards, regulators may respond with more prescriptive oversight and regulatory requirements. Standards and requirements must be grounded in a technical understanding of AI models and agents, including their functionality, training and testing, analysis and prediction capabilities, and susceptibility to manipulation or exploitation.”

“Security leaders need a technical understanding of AI models and agents, including their functionality, training and testing, analysis and prediction capabilities, and susceptibility to attacks, manipulation, or exploitation. They also need to understand how AI agents function within the broader technology environment.”

– Lee Kim, cybersecurity consultant and attorney, and faculty member, IANS

“In 2027, exploitation before a patch exists becomes the default rather than the exception. Mandiant already measured the mean time to exploit at roughly minus seven days in its M-Trends 2026 report, which means attackers were typically inside before defenders had anything to install. As AI agents get better at turning advisories, commits and code diffs into working exploits within hours, that number will move further into negative territory and stay there.”

On that trajectory, 2027 will be the first year in which more than one million vulnerabilities are discovered that should qualify for a CVE.
